A.explanation: Moving away stretches the observed wavelength so $f_o = v/\lambda_{obs}$ is lower than the source frequency.

B.explanation: Moving towards the observer compresses wavefronts and increases observed wavelength denominator, giving a higher observed frequency.

C.explanation: Wave speed in air is fixed by the medium and is not decreased by source motion; source motion changes observed wavelength, not $v$.

D.explanation: Wave speed in air is fixed by the medium and is not increased by source motion; source motion changes observed wavelength, not $v$.

hints: Notice the observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency, so the observed wavelength must be longer with the same wave speed.
Recall for sound that $v = f\lambda$ stays set by air, while source motion shifts successive wavefront positions and changes $\lambda_{obs}$.
Compare stretching of wavefronts when the source recedes with compression when it approaches to decide which motion lowers $f_o$.
walkthrough: Identify the Doppler situation: a moving sound source, stationary observer, and $f_{observed} < f_{source}$.
State the governing rule: wave speed $v$ in air depends on the medium, not on source speed, so $v = f_o \lambda_{obs}$ with constant $v$.
Argue the cause-and-effect: if the source moves away, each new wavefront is emitted further back, so the separation $\lambda_{obs}$ between wavefronts along the line to the observer is increased.
Connect to frequency: larger $\lambda_{obs}$ with the same $v$ gives $f_o = v/\lambda_{obs}$ smaller than the source frequency.
Reject the speed-change ideas because source motion does not change $v$ in air, and reject motion towards the observer because that would shorten $\lambda_{obs}$ and raise $f_o$.
